Cloud GPU Pricing: RunPod, Vultr, DigitalOcean, Lambda, AWS

# Cloud GPU pricing compared: RunPod, Vultr, DigitalOcean, Lambda and AWS, and how to turn an hourly rate into cost per million tokens

David Lewin · Updated October 18, 2026 · 8 min read

## TL;DR

The bottom line, before the detail

On 23 October 2026 an L40S (48 GB) cost $0.79 to $1.09 an hour on RunPod, $1.57 on DigitalOcean, $1.671 on Vultr and $1.861 on demand on AWS (g6e.xlarge); an H100 SXM cost $2.69 to $3.99 on RunPod, $2.99 per GPU in Vultr's 8-GPU server, $3.99 to $4.29 on Lambda and $6.88 per GPU on demand on AWS (p5.48xlarge). The hourly rate is only half the comparison: billing granularity, storage while stopped, minimum terms and above all the tokens per second you actually get decide the price per job. Rent the candidate GPU for an hour, run the benchmark script in this guide at your real concurrency, and divide.

Listen to the audio overview RunPod vs Vultr vs Paperspace: Cloud GPU Pricing Press play to hear it here, without leaving the page

GPU clouds compete on the hourly price because it's the one number that fits in a headline. What you pay for a job depends on four other things: how many tokens or images per second that GPU actually delivers for your model, how billing rounds, what storage costs while the machine is stopped, and whether the GPU you want is available when you need it. This guide gives you the October 2026 list prices, then a way to turn them into cost per million tokens for your own workload.

## List prices on 23 October 2026

On-demand prices per GPU per hour, in US dollars, taken from each provider's pricing page or public API on 23 October 2026. Prices change often; the provider's page wins over this table.

| GPU (VRAM) | RunPod Community / Secure | Vultr | DigitalOcean | Lambda | AWS on demand |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RTX 4090 (24 GB) | $0.34 / $0.89 | n/a | n/a | n/a | n/a |
| RTX 6000 Ada (48 GB) | $0.74 / $0.99 | n/a | $1.57 | n/a | n/a |
| L40S (48 GB) | $0.79 / $1.09 | $1.671 (1 GPU, 16 vCPU, 180 GB RAM) | $1.57 | n/a | $1.861 (g6e.xlarge) |
| A100 80 GB SXM | $1.39 / $1.79 | $2.80 (8-GPU bare metal, $22.40/h) | n/a | $2.79 (8-GPU) | n/a |
| H100 80 GB SXM | $2.69 / $3.99 | $2.99 (8-GPU bare metal, $23.92/h) | $4.41 | $4.29 (1 GPU), $3.99 (8-GPU) | $6.88 (p5.48xlarge, $55.04/h) |
| H200 (141 GB) | $3.59 / $5.29 | n/a | $4.47 | n/a | n/a |
| GH200 (96 GB) | n/a | $1.99 (bare metal) | n/a | $2.29 | n/a |

Sources: RunPod pricing page; Vultr's public plans API (`api.vultr.com/v2/plans` and `/v2/plans-metal`); DigitalOcean's GPU Droplet pricing page; Lambda's pricing page (plus sales tax); AWS prices via instances.vantage.sh for us-east-1 Linux. "n/a" means the GPU wasn't listed as on-demand in that source, not that the provider can never get it. Lambda and DigitalOcean also sell reserved capacity through sales; DigitalOcean lists 12-month H100 contracts at $3.26 per GPU-hour.

Two patterns stand out. The cheapest H100 hours come in 8-GPU servers (Vultr, Lambda) or on marketplace-style capacity (RunPod Community Cloud, which runs on third-party hosts). And AWS on demand is the most expensive way to buy the same silicon; AWS makes sense when the GPU must sit inside an existing AWS account, VPC and compliance boundary, or with Spot and Savings Plans. Its g6e.xlarge listed at $1.568 Spot and $1.172 with a one-year reservation on the same day.

## What the hourly price leaves out

| Item | Why it matters | Examples (October 2026) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Billing granularity | Short jobs on hourly billing pay for unused minutes | RunPod and DigitalOcean bill per second; DigitalOcean has a 5-minute minimum |
| Stopped is not free | A stopped machine can still bill for the GPU or its disk | DigitalOcean bills powered-off GPU Droplets until destroyed; RunPod volumes cost $0.20/GB a month while stopped vs $0.10 running |
| Bundle size | Some GPUs only come 8 at a time | Vultr's H100 and A100 are 8-GPU bare-metal servers, billed monthly or hourly |
| Data transfer | Downloading checkpoints and datasets, serving images | DigitalOcean includes 10,000 to 15,000 GiB per GPU Droplet; check the egress line for the others |
| Interruptions | Spot capacity can be taken back, and the work since the last checkpoint is lost | AWS Spot, DigitalOcean Spot (B300 and MI-series listed); see the rent vs buy cost model for the rework math |
| Host quality | Marketplace hosts vary in network speed, disk and uptime | RunPod Community Cloud, Vast.ai listings |

## Pick the GPU class before the provider

Choosing a provider is easier once you know which GPU class the workload needs. For LLM serving the deciding numbers are memory size (does the model plus KV cache fit) and memory bandwidth (how fast each token is generated). For training and image generation, compute matters more.

| GPU | Memory | Bandwidth | Dense BF16 tensor | Good fit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RTX 4090 | 24 GB GDDR6X | 1,008 GB/s | ~165 TFLOPS | 7-8B models quantized, SDXL and FLUX in FP8, LoRA on small models |
| L40S | 48 GB GDDR6 | 864 GB/s | ~362 TFLOPS | Image generation, 8-14B models in BF16, 70B in 4-bit for one or two users |
| RTX 6000 Ada | 48 GB GDDR6 | 960 GB/s | ~364 TFLOPS | Same class as the L40S |
| A100 80 GB SXM | 80 GB HBM2e | 2,039 GB/s | 312 TFLOPS | Fine-tuning, 70B quantized with many users, mature software support |
| H100 80 GB SXM | 80 GB HBM3 | 3,350 GB/s | ~989 TFLOPS | High-throughput serving and training, FP8 |
| H200 | 141 GB HBM3e | 4,800 GB/s | ~989 TFLOPS | 70B in BF16 on one GPU, long contexts |

Figures are from NVIDIA datasheets (dense, without sparsity; the RTX 4090 figure is with FP32 accumulate). The VRAM calculator tells you which rows fit your model and context.

## Turn hourly prices into cost per million tokens

The only number that compares an RTX 4090 at $0.34 with an H100 at $2.69 is cost per unit of work. For text, that's cost per million output tokens at the concurrency you actually run:

`cost per 1M tokens = hourly price ÷ (aggregate tokens per second × 3,600) × 1,000,000`

Aggregate tokens per second depends on the model, the serving engine, the prompt and output lengths and the number of parallel requests, so measure it. Rent each candidate GPU for an hour, start vLLM with your model, and run this against it with prompts like your real ones:
